scope_allowed: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

models.name: HH-Explicit
models.what_it_computes: Coupled helmet–head explicit finite element analysis of skull stress fields and whole-head linear and angular kinematics with helmet structural and contact response

models.name: BH-Explicit
models.what_it_computes: Bare-head explicit finite element analysis resolving skull strain and brain deformation metrics (e.g., peak principal strain proxies and relative brain–skull motion) without helmet influence

mechanisms.name: Linear drop to rigid anvil
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Dominated by translational deceleration and normal contact, it governs skull stress and peak linear head acceleration relevant to skull fracture and focal injury thresholds

mechanisms.name: Oblique impact with tangential load
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Produces coupled normal–tangential loading and head rotation, governing angular kinematics and brain shear deformation associated with diffuse injury risk

deviation.detail: Credibility scores reported on a 0–5 scale per factor and per (model × mechanism) pair, where higher values denote stronger evidence

expected_decision.outcome_source: In the round, these outcomes justify the medium model risk designation and the use of simulations to winnow the design space and to contextualize test results without supplanting them.
rationale_keywords: used to winnow the design space

expected_context_of_use: In practice, the models are used to predict skull stress and brain-relevant kinematics across standardized linear and oblique impacts and to demonstrate performance against predefined acceptance thresholds.

spans: During validation planning we recognized that several laboratory parameters do not translate uniquely into model inputs.
We therefore documented input ranges and, where practical, bounded their influence through sensitivity screens; however, a full equivalence demonstration was not the goal of this exercise.

spans: For HH-Explicit under linear drop, the refinement pro-cess produced small changes in the two most decision-relevant outputs: the grid convergence index (GCI) was 3.6% for peak resultant head acceleration and 4.2% for peak skull von Mises stress.

Mesh studies produced small changes in key outputs in the linear regime (e.g., 3.6% grid convergence index, GCI, for peak head acceleration in HH-Explicit) and moderate changes in oblique loading (e.g., 7.8% GCI for peak angular acceleration in HH-Explicit), leading to higher confidence for linear conditions.

spans: Benchmarks and manufactured-solution tests showed small departures from reference behavior for both models’ solvers and contact algorithms (<0.5%–0.8% across tests).

spans: HH-Explicit comprises a helmet shell and liner assembled over a human head model rooted in modern cranial anatomy.

The slip interface is implemented as a penalty-based surface with an asymptotic transition from static to kinetic shear resistance and kinematics-driven weakening to capture micro-slip preceding running slip.

spans: During validation planning we recognized that several laboratory parameters do not translate uniquely into model inputs.

The slip interface’s effective shear resistance may depend on contact pressure and transient microslip, abrasive surface clogging can change kinetic friction during a test sequence, and donor variability in skull thickness and suture morphology is imperfectly represented in a nominal skull model.

spans: The brain is represented by a nearly incompressible visco-hyperelastic law with shear relaxation times spanning 0.1–100 ms and a low-frequency storage modulus of 0.6–0.8 kPa, consistent with rheometry and inverse identification from kinematics.
